en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Jewels 85.
The Training Rule on Entering a Village at an Improper Time.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks entered a village at an improper time, sat down in the assembly hall, and engaged in various kinds of frivolous talk,
namely: talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drinks,
talk of clothes, talk of beds, talk of garlands, talk of perfumes, talk of relatives, and talk of vehicles.
Talk about villages, talk about market towns, talk about cities, talk about the countryside, talk about women, talk about heroes, talk about streets, talk about wells,
talk about departed ancestors, talk about various matters, talk about speculations concerning the world, talk about speculations concerning the ocean,
or talk about "thus it was" and "thus it will be. People criticize, grumble, and complain:

“How can the recluses, sons of the Sakyans, enter a village at an improper time, sit in the assembly hall, and engage in various kinds of frivolous talk, such as talk about kings, talk about thieves, ... [and so on] ...
talk about whether things exist or do not exist after death, just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures?”
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... they grumbled, complained, and criticized:
"How can the group-of-six monks, having entered a village at an improper time and sat down in the assembly hall, engage in various kinds of frivolous talk, such as this?"
“Talk about kings, talk about thieves … [and so on] … talk about ‘thus it was’ or ‘thus it will be’?
… “Is it true, monks, that you enter the village at the wrong time, sit in the assembly hall, and engage in various kinds of frivolous talk, such as this:”
“Talk of kings, talk of thieves... [and so on] ...
or talk of ‘thus it was’ and ‘thus it will be’?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, having entered a village at an improper time and sat down in the assembly hall, engage in various kinds of frivolous talk,
such as talk about kings, talk about thieves, and so forth?”
Or talk about existence and non-existence.
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whosoever, however, a bhikkhu should enter a village at an improper time, it is an offense entailing expiation.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus traveling through the Kosala country toward Sāvatthī arrived at a certain village in the evening.
When people saw those bhikkhus, they said to them,
“Enter, venerable sirs.
Then those bhikkhus—
Thinking, “The Blessed One has prohibited entering a village at an improper time,” they did not enter out of scrupulousness.
Robbers robbed those bhikkhus.
Then those bhikkhus went to Sāvatthī and reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the monks:
“I allow you, monks, to enter a village at an improper time after having requested permission.”
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whosoever, however, a monk should enter a village at an improper time without having informed [another], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
In this way, this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu traveling from the Kosala country toward Sāvatthī arrived at a certain village in the evening.
When the people saw him, they said to him,
“Enter, venerable sir.”
Then that bhikkhu,
being anxious because "the Blessed One has prohibited entering a village at an improper time without having asked permission," did not enter.
Robbers robbed that bhikkhu.
Then that bhikkhu went to Sāvatthī and reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this context, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, monks, having asked permission from a monk who is present, to enter a village at an improper time.
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
‘Whosoever monk, not having asked permission from a monk who is present, should enter a village at an improper time, it is an offense of expiation.’”
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, a certain monk had been bitten by a snake.
Another monk went to the village, thinking, "I shall bring fire."

Then that bhikkhu, being anxious because he thought, "The Blessed One has prohibited entering a village at an improper time without having asked permission from a bhikkhu who is present," did not enter. ...
[They] reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this context, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, when there is an urgent business of such a kind, to enter a village at an improper time without having asked permission from a bhikkhu who is present.
And furthermore, bhikkhus, you should recite this training rule thus:”

“Whatever bhikkhu, however, should enter a village at an improper time without having informed a bhikkhu who is present—except in the case of such urgent business as that—it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
“Whatever bhikkhu” means whichever one... [and so forth].
“Bhikkhu” … [as before] … this is the type of bhikkhu intended in this context.
A “peaceful” bhikkhu is one—
It is possible for a virtuous bhikkhu to enter after having asked for permission.
An unvirtuous bhikkhu, however,
is not able to enter even after asking for permission.
"Improper time" means from when the midday has passed until the rising of the sun.
"Should enter a village" means...
For one who crosses the boundary of an enclosed village, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
For one who enters the vicinity of an unenclosed village, there is an offense of expiation—
unless it is for such an urgent business.
Except when there is such an urgent business.

If, at an improper time, perceiving it to be an improper time, he enters a village without having asked permission from a monk who is present—unless there is such an urgent business—he commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).

If, at an improper time, being in doubt, he enters a village without having asked permission from a monk who is present—unless there is such an urgent business—he commits an offense entailing confession.

If, perceiving it to be the wrong time when it is actually the right time, a monk enters a village without having asked permission from a monk who is present—except in the case of such an urgent business—he commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
If he perceives it to be the wrong time when it is actually the right time, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he is in doubt as to whether it is the right time, he commits an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives it as the right time when it is the right time,
there is no offense.
There is no offense in the case of such urgent business.
He enters after asking permission from a monk who is present,
he enters without asking permission from a monk who is absent,
and he goes to the interior of the monastery.
She goes to a nunnery,
she goes to the lodgings of non-Buddhist ascetics,
she goes to a place of retreat.
The path is [open] within a village,
in times of distress,
and for one who is insane.
"For one who is a first-offender":
the third training rule concerning entering a village at an improper time is finished.
